claim: Dynamin is a mechanochemical GTPase essential for membrane fission during clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
source: Dynamin is a mechanochemical GTPase essential for membrane fission during clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by extensive prior research and cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dynamin forms helical complexes at the neck of clathrin-coated pits.
source: Dynamin forms helical complexes at the neck of clathrin-coated pits and their structural changes coupled with GTP hydrolysis drive membrane fission.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Structural changes of dynamin coupled with GTP hydrolysis drive membrane fission.
source: Dynamin forms helical complexes at the neck of clathrin-coated pits and their structural changes coupled with GTP hydrolysis drive membrane fission.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by prior research and is the basis for the current study.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin helices are rearranged to form clusters upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: HS-AFM analyses show that the dynamin-amphiphysin helices are rearranged to form clusters upon GTP hydrolysis and membrane constriction occurs at protein-uncoated regions flanking the clusters.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by HS-AFM imaging data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Membrane constriction occurs at protein-uncoated regions flanking the dynamin-amphiphysin clusters.
source: HS-AFM analyses show that the dynamin-amphiphysin helices are rearranged to form clusters upon GTP hydrolysis and membrane constriction occurs at protein-uncoated regions flanking the clusters.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 4 showing constriction at flanking regions.

claim: Amphiphysin has a novel function in size control of dynamin-amphiphysin clusters.
source: We also show a novel function of amphiphysin in size control of the clusters to enhance biogenesis of endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EM data in Figure 5 comparing cluster sizes with and without amphiphysin.

claim: Amphiphysin enhances biogenesis of endocytic vesicles through cluster size control.
source: We also show a novel function of amphiphysin in size control of the clusters to enhance biogenesis of endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing smaller vesicles and shorter intervals between constriction sites with amphiphysin (Figure 5).

claim: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the best characterized endocytic pathway.
source: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME) is the best characterized endocytic pathway by which cells incorporate extracellular molecules into cells as cargoes of clathrin-coated vesicles (Kirchhausen et al., 2014; McMahon and Boucrot, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citations.

claim: CME is required for neuronal transmission, signal transduction, cell adhesion and migration.
source: CME is required for various essential processes including neuronal transmission, signal transduction and other cell membrane activities such as cell adhesion and migration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biological importance of CME.

claim: There are three dynamin isoforms in mammals.
source: There are three dynamin isoforms in mammals: dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, two tissue-specific isoforms which are highly expressed in neurons, and dynamin 2, an ubiquitously expressed isoform (Cao et al., 1998; Cook et al., 1996, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynamin 1 and dynamin 3 are tissue-specific isoforms highly expressed in neurons.
source: There are three dynamin isoforms in mammals: dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, two tissue-specific isoforms which are highly expressed in neurons, and dynamin 2, an ubiquitously expressed isoform (Cao et al., 1998; Cook et al., 1996, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynamin 2 is an ubiquitously expressed isoform.
source: There are three dynamin isoforms in mammals: dynamin 1 and dynamin 3, two tissue-specific isoforms which are highly expressed in neurons, and dynamin 2, an ubiquitously expressed isoform (Cao et al., 1998; Cook et al., 1996, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynamin consists of five structurally distinct domains: a GTPase domain, a bundle signaling element (BSE), a stalk, a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain and a proline-rich domain (PRD).
source: Structural studies from several groups demonstrated that dynamin consists of five structurally distinct domains: a GTPase domain, a bundle signaling element (BSE), a stalk, a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain and a proline-rich domain (PRD) from N-terminus to C-terminus (Faelber et al., 2011; Ford et al., 2011; Reubold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The GTPase domain is responsible for hydrolysis of GTP.
source: The GTPase domain is responsible for hydrolysis of GTP (guanosine triphosphate) and the PH domain is required for membrane association by binding to negatively charged phospholipids such as PI (4,5) P2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynamin domain functions.

claim: The PH domain is required for membrane association by binding to negatively charged phospholipids such as PI(4,5)P2.
source: The GTPase domain is responsible for hydrolysis of GTP (guanosine triphosphate) and the PH domain is required for membrane association by binding to negatively charged phospholipids such as PI (4,5) P2 (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynamin domain functions.

claim: The stalk structure serves as a binding interface for dimerization and oligomerization of dynamin.
source: The stalk structure serves as a binding interface for dimerization and oligomerization of dynamin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynamin structure and function.

claim: The BSE functions as a flexible hinge required for structural changes of dynamin upon GTP hydrolysis.
source: The BSE, which is located between the stalk and GTPase domain, functions as a flexible hinge required for structural changes of dynamin upon GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dynamin domain functions.

claim: Dynamin helical oligomers were first observed in presynaptic terminals of shibire mutant flies at restrictive temperature.
source: Dynamin forms helical oligomers which was first observed in presynaptic terminals of shibire mutant flies at restrictive temperature (Koenig and Ikeda, 1989).
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citation.

claim: Dynamin assembles into helices at the neck of endocytic pits in isolated presynaptic nerve terminals treated with GTPγS.
source: Dynamin also assembles into helices at the neck of endocytic pits in the isolated presynaptic nerve terminals treated with slowly hydrolyzable GTP analogue GTPγS (guanosine 5'-O-[gamma-thio]triphosphate) (Takei et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dynamin helices can be reconstituted in vitro with liposomes.
source: Similar dynamin helices were reconstituted in vitro either with liposomes (Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998; Takei et al., 1998) or without liposomes in a low-salt condition (Hinshaw and Schmid, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Dynamin helices can be reconstituted in vitro without liposomes in a low-salt condition.
source: Similar dynamin helices were reconstituted in vitro either with liposomes (Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998; Takei et al., 1998) or without liposomes in a low-salt condition (Hinshaw and Schmid, 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Membrane constriction is required, but not sufficient, for fission.
source: There is a consensus view about the dynamin-mediated membrane constriction and fission which is well supported by previous studies from different groups: membrane constriction is required, but not sufficient, for fission (Antonny et al., 2016; Faelber et al., 2012; Schmid and Frolov, 2011).
evidence: This is a consensus view in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is controversial how membrane constriction is achieved by dynamin.
source: However, it is still controversial how constriction is achieved, and what GTP energy is used for.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of debate in the field.

claim: It is controversial what GTP energy is used for in dynamin-mediated membrane fission.
source: However, it is still controversial how constriction is achieved, and what GTP energy is used for.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of debate in the field.

claim: Membrane constriction could be achieved by assembly into the highly constricted state when dynamin is bound to GTP.
source: For example, membrane constriction could be achieved by assembly into the highly constricted state when dynamin is bound to GTP (Chen et al., 2004; Mattila et al., 2015; Mears et al., 2007; Zhang and Hinshaw, 2001).
evidence: This is one proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Membrane constriction could be achieved by hydrolysis of GTP that induces a conformational change leading to constriction.
source: Alternatively, membrane constriction could be achieved by hydrolysis of GTP that induces a conformational change leading to constriction (Cocucci et al., 2014; Marks et al., 2001; Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an alternative proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Amphiphysin is a BAR domain protein required for membrane invagination in CME.
source: Amphiphysin is a BAR domain protein required for membrane invagination in CME (Wigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Amphiphysin has a lipid interacting BAR domain in its N-terminal, a medial clathrin/AP-2 binding (CLAP) domain and C-terminal Src homology 3 (SH3) domain.
source: Amphiphysin has a lipid interacting BAR (Bin–Amphiphysin–Rvs) domain in its N-terminal, a medial clathrin/AP-2 binding (CLAP) domain and C-terminal Src homology 3 (SH3) domain.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about amphiphysin.

claim: The BAR domain of amphiphysin forms crescent-shaped dimer.
source: The BAR domain of amphiphysin forms crescent-shaped dimer and its concave surface serves as a platform for bending membrane or sensing membrane curvature (Peter et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The concave surface of the BAR domain serves as a platform for bending membrane or sensing membrane curvature.
source: The BAR domain of amphiphysin forms crescent-shaped dimer and its concave surface serves as a platform for bending membrane or sensing membrane curvature (Peter et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The CLAP domain binds to clathrin and AP-2.
source: The CLAP domain binds to clathrin and AP-2, major components of clathrin-coated pits, and helps to recruit amphiphysin to the sites of CME.
evidence: This is established knowledge about amphiphysin domain functions.

claim: The CLAP domain helps to recruit amphiphysin to the sites of CME.
source: The CLAP domain binds to clathrin and AP-2, major components of clathrin-coated pits, and helps to recruit amphiphysin to the sites of CME.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding function of the CLAP domain.

claim: The C-terminal SH3 domain of amphiphysin binds directly to the PRD of dynamin 1.
source: In addition, the C-terminal SH3 domain of amphiphysin binds directly to the PRD of dynamin 1 (David et al., 1996; Takei et al., 1999) and enhances dynamin's GTPase activity in the presence of liposomes (Takei et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The SH3 domain of amphiphysin enhances dynamin's GTPase activity in the presence of liposomes.
source: In addition, the C-terminal SH3 domain of amphiphysin binds directly to the PRD of dynamin 1 (David et al., 1996; Takei et al., 1999) and enhances dynamin's GTPase activity in the presence of liposomes (Takei et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Amphiphysin copolymerizes with dynamin 1 into helical complexes which form membrane tubules in vitro.
source: Amphiphysin copolymerizes with dynamin 1 into helical complexes, which form membrane tubules in vitro (Takei et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2004) similar to those formed from synaptic plasma membranes (Takei et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Injection of specific antibodies against amphiphysin into the giant synapse in lampreys causes suppressed endocytosis in synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: Furthermore, injection of specific antibodies against amphiphysin into the giant synapse in lampreys (Evergren et al., 2004) or amphiphysin KO in mice (Di Paolo et al., 2002) causes suppressed endocytosis in synaptic vesicle recycling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Amphiphysin KO in mice causes suppressed endocytosis in synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: Furthermore, injection of specific antibodies against amphiphysin into the giant synapse in lampreys (Evergren et al., 2004) or amphiphysin KO in mice (Di Paolo et al., 2002) causes suppressed endocytosis in synaptic vesicle recycling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Dynamin mediates membrane fission in CME in collaboration with amphiphysin in vivo.
source: These results suggest that dynamin mediates membrane fission in CME in collaboration with amphiphysin in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies showing functional importance of amphiphysin.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes induced tubulation of large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) in the absence of GTP.
source: As previously described (Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998; Takei et al., 1999), the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes induced tubulation of large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) in the absence of GTP (Figure 1A, No GTP) and it is not stoichiometry dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1A and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: Tubulation of LUVs by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes is not stoichiometry dependent.
source: As previously described (Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998; Takei et al., 1999), the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes induced tubulation of large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) in the absence of GTP (Figure 1A, No GTP) and it is not stoichiometry dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Lipid tubules started to form multiple constriction sites over time after GTP addition.
source: Immediately after the addition of 1 mM GTP, the appearance of lipid tubules was not affected (Figure 1A, GTP 1 s), but they started to form multiple constriction sites over time (Figure 1A, GTP 5 s, 10 s and 30 s) and membrane fission occurred finally and numerous vesicles were generated within 1 min (Figure 1A, GTP 1 min).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by EM time course data in Figure 1A.

claim: Membrane fission occurred and numerous vesicles were generated within 1 min after GTP addition.
source: Immediately after the addition of 1 mM GTP, the appearance of lipid tubules was not affected (Figure 1A, GTP 1 s), but they started to form multiple constriction sites over time (Figure 1A, GTP 5 s, 10 s and 30 s) and membrane fission occurred finally and numerous vesicles were generated within 1 min (Figure 1A, GTP 1 min).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by EM time course data in Figure 1A.

claim: Membrane fission activity by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was stoichiometry sensitive.
source: The membrane fission activity by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was stoichiometry sensitive: the membrane fission occurred efficiently at 1:0.5 or 1:1 molar ratio of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:0.5 and 1:1), while the fission activity was less efficient when dynamin and amphiphysin were mixed at 1:2 ratio (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:2), probably due to lower stimulatory effect of amphiphysin on dynamin GTPase activity at the higher molecular ratio (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Membrane fission occurred efficiently at 1:0.5 or 1:1 molar ratio of dynamin and amphiphysin.
source: The membrane fission activity by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was stoichiometry sensitive: the membrane fission occurred efficiently at 1:0.5 or 1:1 molar ratio of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:0.5 and 1:1), while the fission activity was less efficient when dynamin and amphiphysin were mixed at 1:2 ratio (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:2), probably due to lower stimulatory effect of amphiphysin on dynamin GTPase activity at the higher molecular ratio (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Fission activity was less efficient when dynamin and amphiphysin were mixed at 1:2 ratio.
source: The membrane fission activity by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was stoichiometry sensitive: the membrane fission occurred efficiently at 1:0.5 or 1:1 molar ratio of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:0.5 and 1:1), while the fission activity was less efficient when dynamin and amphiphysin were mixed at 1:2 ratio (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:2), probably due to lower stimulatory effect of amphiphysin on dynamin GTPase activity at the higher molecular ratio (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Lower fission efficiency at 1:2 ratio is probably due to lower stimulatory effect of amphiphysin on dynamin GTPase activity at the higher molecular ratio.
source: The membrane fission activity by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was stoichiometry sensitive: the membrane fission occurred efficiently at 1:0.5 or 1:1 molar ratio of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:0.5 and 1:1), while the fission activity was less efficient when dynamin and amphiphysin were mixed at 1:2 ratio (Figure 1-figure supplement 2C, 1:2), probably due to lower stimulatory effect of amphiphysin on dynamin GTPase activity at the higher molecular ratio (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The appearance of lipid tubules was not affected in the presence of GTPγS.
source: The appearance of lipid tubules (Figure 1B, No GTP) was not affected in the presence of either slowly hydrolyzable GTP analogue GTPγS (Figure 1B, GTPγS) or non-hydrolyzable GTP analogue GMP-PNP (guanosine 5′-[β,γ-imido]triphosphate) (Figure 1B, GMP-PNP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: The appearance of lipid tubules was not affected in the presence of GMP-PNP.
source: The appearance of lipid tubules (Figure 1B, No GTP) was not affected in the presence of either slowly hydrolyzable GTP analogue GTPγS (Figure 1B, GTPγS) or non-hydrolyzable GTP analogue GMP-PNP (guanosine 5′-[β,γ-imido]triphosphate) (Figure 1B, GMP-PNP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: In the presence of GDP and vanadate, lipid tubules were constricted at multiple sites.
source: In contrast, in the presence of GDP (guanosine diphosphate) and vanadate, the complex which mimics the GDP⋅Pi transition state, lipid tubules were constricted at multiple sites (Figure 1B, GDP + vanadate).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: GDP and vanadate mimics the GDP⋅Pi transition state.
source: In contrast, in the presence of GDP (guanosine diphosphate) and vanadate, the complex which mimics the GDP⋅Pi transition state, lipid tubules were constricted at multiple sites (Figure 1B, GDP + vanadate).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GDP-vanadate as a transition state analog.

claim: Addition of only GDP did not cause membrane constriction or fission, but membrane tubules were deformed.
source: Addition of only GDP did not cause membrane constriction or fission, but membrane tubules were deformed (Figure 1B, GDP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: Numerous vesicles were generated 10 min after the addition of 1 mM GTP.
source: Finally, numerous vesicles were generated 10 min after the addition of 1 mM GTP, in which multiple rounds of GTP hydrolysis were likely to have taken place (Figure 1B, GTP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: Multiple rounds of GTP hydrolysis were likely to have taken place 10 min after GTP addition.
source: Finally, numerous vesicles were generated 10 min after the addition of 1 mM GTP, in which multiple rounds of GTP hydrolysis were likely to have taken place (Figure 1B, GTP).
evidence: This is inferred from the time course and the observation of vesicle formation.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is essential for both membrane constriction and fission by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes.
source: Taken these results together, GTP hydrolysis is essential for both membrane constriction and fission by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes, but subsequent dissociation of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is required for completing membrane fission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EM data in Figure 1B showing effects of different nucleotide states.

claim: Subsequent dissociation of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is required for completing membrane fission.
source: Taken these results together, GTP hydrolysis is essential for both membrane constriction and fission by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes, but subsequent dissociation of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is required for completing membrane fission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EM data showing constriction with GDP-vanadate but fission only with GTP.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes assembled into helices on the lipid nanotubes.
source: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes assembled into helices on the lipid nanotubes (Figure 2A, No GTP), which is similar to those formed by dynamin alone (Stowell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 2A.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin helices on lipid nanotubes are similar to those formed by dynamin alone.
source: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes assembled into helices on the lipid nanotubes (Figure 2A, No GTP), which is similar to those formed by dynamin alone (Stowell et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited prior work and EM data.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices transiently formed clusters after the addition of GTP.
source: Interestingly, the dynamin-amphiphysin helices transiently formed clusters after the addition of GTP (Figure 2A, GTP 1 s and 20 s, brackets).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by EM time course data in Figure 2A.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin clusters were disorganized over time and partially dissociated from the nanotubes.
source: The dynamin-amphiphysin clusters were disorganized over time and partially dissociated from the nanotubes (Figure 2A, GTP 30 s and 1 min).
evidence: This is supported by EM time course data in Figure 2A.

claim: The appearance of dynamin-amphiphysin helices was unchanged in the presence of GTPγS or GMP-PNP.
source: The appearance of dynamin-amphiphysin helices was unchanged even in the presence of GTPγS or GMP-PNP (Figure 2B, No GTP, GTPγS and GMP-PNP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of GDP and vanadate induced rearrangement of the dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes to form clusters.
source: Interestingly, addition of GDP and vanadate induced rearrangement of the dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes to form clusters similar to those observed after the addition of GTP (Figure 2B, GDP + vanadate).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: The average pitch of helices in the clusters was 15.0 ± 0.3 nm.
source: The average pitch of helices in the clusters were shorter (15.0 ± 0.3 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) compared to the average pitch of the helical complexes in No GTP control (20.0 ± 0.5 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data.

claim: The average pitch of the helical complexes in No GTP control was 20.0 ± 0.5 nm.
source: The average pitch of helices in the clusters were shorter (15.0 ± 0.3 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) compared to the average pitch of the helical complexes in No GTP control (20.0 ± 0.5 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data.

claim: GDP alone did not affect the distribution of dynamin-amphiphysin helices.
source: In contrast, GDP alone did not affect the distribution of dynamin-amphiphysin helices (Figure 2B, GDP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes were disorganized and eventually dissociated from the lipid nanotubes 10 min after the addition of 1 mM GTP.
source: Finally, the dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes were disorganized and eventually dissociated from the lipid nanotubes 10 min after the addition of 1 mM GTP (Figure 2B, GTP).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 2B.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes transiently form clusters in the GTP hydrolysis transition state of GDP⋅Pi during which membrane tubules are constricted.
source: Taken these results together, the dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes transiently form clusters in the GTP hydrolysis transition state of GDP⋅Pi during which membrane tubules are constricted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EM data showing clustering with GDP-vanadate.

claim: Clustering behavior of the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes on the lipid nanotubes was not stoichiometry dependent.
source: Furthermore, unlike membrane fission activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), clustering behavior of the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes on the lipid nanotubes were not stoichiometry dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 1:0.5, 1:1 and 1:2, white brackets).
evidence: This is supported by EM data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LUVs were stably immobilized on the carbon-coated and glow-discharged mica substrate.
source: LUVs were stably immobilized on the carbon-coated and glow-discharged mica substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Video 1), and they were successfully tubulated in the presence of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and Video 1.

claim: LUVs were successfully tubulated in the presence of dynamin and amphiphysin.
source: LUVs were stably immobilized on the carbon-coated and glow-discharged mica substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Video 1), and they were successfully tubulated in the presence of dynamin and amphiphysin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Video 2.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices on the lipid tubules were aligned with an almost regular pitch of 22.0 ± 0.7 nm.
source: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices on the lipid tubules were aligned with an almost regular pitch (22.0 ± 0.7 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) and they were immobile before GTP addition (Figure 3A, 0 s and 21 s; Video 3; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from HS-AFM data in Figure 3A.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices were immobile before GTP addition.
source: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices on the lipid tubules were aligned with an almost regular pitch (22.0 ± 0.7 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) and they were immobile before GTP addition (Figure 3A, 0 s and 21 s; Video 3; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin helices became mobile after GTP addition and eventually formed clusters consisting of a few helices with shorter pitch of 15.7 ± 0.3 nm.
source: Interestingly, the dynamin-amphiphysin helices became mobile after GTP addition and eventually formed clusters consisting of a few helices with shorter pitch (15.7 ± 0.3 nm, mean pitch ± s.e.m.) (Figure 3A, from 42 s to 131 s; Video 3; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes were static before GTP addition.
source: Particle tracking analyses of the individual dynamin-amphiphysin helices showed that the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes were static before GTP addition (Figure 3B, 5-21 s; Video 4), but addition of 1 mM GTP stimulated longitudinal movement of the helical complexes, leading to the cluster formation (Figure 3B, 38-54 s, 38–86 s and 38–118 s; Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by particle tracking analysis in Figure 3B and Video 4.

claim: Addition of 1 mM GTP stimulated longitudinal movement of the helical complexes, leading to the cluster formation.
source: Particle tracking analyses of the individual dynamin-amphiphysin helices showed that the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes were static before GTP addition (Figure 3B, 5-21 s; Video 4), but addition of 1 mM GTP stimulated longitudinal movement of the helical complexes, leading to the cluster formation (Figure 3B, 38-54 s, 38–86 s and 38–118 s; Video 5).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by particle tracking analysis in Figure 3B and Video 5.

claim: The helices had a tendency to constrict during the cluster formation.
source: Although membrane fission was not observed in this sample probably due to a strong attachment of the lipid tubule to the substrate, the helices had a tendency to constrict during the cluster formation (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—source data 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by height measurements in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Membrane fission was not observed in this sample probably due to a strong attachment of the lipid tubule to the substrate.
source: Although membrane fission was not observed in this sample probably due to a strong attachment of the lipid tubule to the substrate, the helices had a tendency to constrict during the cluster formation (Figure 3C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3—source data 2; Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed fission.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes undergo two modes of structural changes: longitudinal clustering and radial constriction during GTP hydrolysis.
source: These results suggest that dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes undergo two modes of structural changes, longitudinal clustering and radial constriction, during GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HS-AFM data showing both types of movements.

claim: A few dynamin-amphiphysin helices merged to form a cluster over time after GTP addition.
source: In the representative sample in which membrane constriction and fission occurred, a few dynamin-amphiphysin helices merged to form a cluster over time after GTP addition (Figure 4A, 0 s, 125.3 s, 185.5 s and 227.5 s; Video 6; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by HS-AFM time course data in Figure 4A and Video 6.

claim: Membrane constriction occurred at flanking regions of the cluster where membrane was bare of dynamin-amphiphysin complexes.
source: Interestingly, membrane constriction occurred at flanking regions of the cluster where membrane was bare of dynamin-amphiphysin complexes (Figure 4A, fission point (FP).1 and FP.2).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 4A.

claim: The heights at sites marked with FP.1 and FP.2 were not changed before constriction.
source: The heights at sites marked with FP.1 and FP.2 were not changed before constriction (Figure 4B, before constriction; Figure 4—source data 2), but they became lower in a stepwise manner from a pre-constriction height of around 30 nm down to 20–25 nm or below (Figure 4B, after constriction; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by height profile data in Figure 4B.

claim: The heights at FP.1 and FP.2 became lower in a stepwise manner from around 30 nm down to 20–25 nm or below after constriction.
source: The heights at sites marked with FP.1 and FP.2 were not changed before constriction (Figure 4B, before constriction; Figure 4—source data 2), but they became lower in a stepwise manner from a pre-constriction height of around 30 nm down to 20–25 nm or below (Figure 4B, after constriction; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by height profile data in Figure 4B.

claim: Membrane constriction and fission occur at the protein-uncoated regions created as a result of the clustering of dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes.
source: These results strongly suggest that membrane constriction and fission occur at the protein-uncoated regions created as a result of the clustering of dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HS-AFM data in Figure 4 showing constriction at bare membrane regions.

claim: The average size of vesicles formed by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was 70.0 ± 2.9 nm.
source: In this study, we also noticed that the average size of vesicles formed by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes (70.0 ± 2.9 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) was significantly smaller compared to those formed by dynamin alone (204.6 ± 12.3 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) after GTP addition (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data in Figure 5A.

claim: The average size of vesicles formed by dynamin alone was 204.6 ± 12.3 nm.
source: In this study, we also noticed that the average size of vesicles formed by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes (70.0 ± 2.9 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) was significantly smaller compared to those formed by dynamin alone (204.6 ± 12.3 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) after GTP addition (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data in Figure 5A.

claim: Vesicles formed by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes were significantly smaller compared to those formed by dynamin alone.
source: In this study, we also noticed that the average size of vesicles formed by dynamin-amphiphysin complexes (70.0 ± 2.9 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) was significantly smaller compared to those formed by dynamin alone (204.6 ± 12.3 nm, mean diameter ± s.e.m.) after GTP addition (Figure 5A; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of EM data in Figure 5A.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin complex formed constriction sites with shorter intervals (150.3 ± 9.8 nm) compared to those formed by dynamin alone (193.5 ± 15.8 nm) in the presence of GDP and vanadate.
source: Consistently, dynamin-amphiphysin complex formed constriction sites with shorter intervals (150.3 ± 9.8 nm, mean intervals ± s.e.m.) compared to those formed by dynamin alone (193.5 ± 15.8 nm, mean intervals ± s.e.m.) in the presence of GDP and vanadate (Figure 5B; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data in Figure 5B.

claim: Dynamin-amphiphysin complexes formed clusters with a mean size of 34.2 ± 1.7 nm in the presence of GDP and vanadate.
source: As already described, dynamin-amphiphysin complexes formed clusters with a few helices in the presence of GDP and vanadate (34.2 ± 1.7 nm, mean cluster size ± s.e.m.) (Figure 5C, Dynamin + Amphiphysin; Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data in Figure 5C.

claim: Dynamin alone formed larger-sized clusters with a mean size of 59.3 ± 4.7 nm.
source: In contrast, dynamin alone formed larger-sized clusters consist of more helical complexes (59.3 ± 4.7 nm, mean cluster size ± s.e.m.) (Figure 5C, Dynamin; Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from EM data in Figure 5C.

claim: Amphiphysin contributes to the effective generation of properly sized vesicles by controlling the cluster formation of dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes.
source: These results suggest that amphiphysin contributes to the effective generation of properly sized vesicles by controlling the cluster formation of dynamin-amphiphysin helical complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 5 showing smaller clusters and vesicles with amphiphysin.

claim: Membrane tubules are constricted in the presence of non-hydrolyzable GTP analogue.
source: Membrane tubules are constricted in the presence of non-hydrolyzable GTP analogue (Chen et al., 2004; Mears et al., 2007; Zhang and Hinshaw, 2001) and more constricted with a GTP-loaded GTPase defective K44A mutant (Sundborger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Membrane tubules are more constricted with a GTP-loaded GTPase defective K44A mutant.
source: Membrane tubules are constricted in the presence of non-hydrolyzable GTP analogue (Chen et al., 2004; Mears et al., 2007; Zhang and Hinshaw, 2001) and more constricted with a GTP-loaded GTPase defective K44A mutant (Sundborger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citation.

claim: Membrane tubules are evenly constricted with non-hydrolyzable GTP analogues and periodical membrane constriction sites which lead to membrane fission are not created.
source: In both cases, membrane tubules are evenly constricted and periodical membrane constriction sites which lead to membrane fission is not created.
evidence: This is a statement about prior observations in the field.

claim: Membrane constriction sites are created in the presence of GDP and vanadate.
source: In the present study, we showed that membrane constriction sites are created in the presence of GDP and vanadate, which mimicked a transition state of GTP hydrolysis (GDP⋅Pi), suggesting that complete hydrolysis of GTP is required for the formation of constriction sites leading to membrane fission (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by EM data in Figure 1B.

claim: Complete hydrolysis of GTP is required for the formation of constriction sites leading to membrane fission.
source: In the present study, we showed that membrane constriction sites are created in the presence of GDP and vanadate, which mimicked a transition state of GTP hydrolysis (GDP⋅Pi), suggesting that complete hydrolysis of GTP is required for the formation of constriction sites leading to membrane fission (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the EM data showing constriction with GDP-vanadate.

claim: Membrane fission has never been observed in the presence of GDP and vanadate.
source: Membrane fission has never been observed in the presence of GDP and vanadate, suggesting that release of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is a prerequisite for membrane fission.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study and prior work.

claim: Release of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is a prerequisite for membrane fission.
source: Membrane fission has never been observed in the presence of GDP and vanadate, suggesting that release of GTP hydrolytic products (GDP and/or phosphate) is a prerequisite for membrane fission.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fission does not occur with GDP-vanadate.

claim: The super-constricted state of dynamin does not constrict the membrane sufficiently enough to reach the hemi-fission state.
source: For instance, the super-constricted state of dynamin does not constrict the membrane sufficiently enough to reach the hemi-fission state (Sundborger et al., 2014) and membrane tension and/or torsion is required to overcome the energy barrier to fission (Bashkirov et al., 2008; Morlot et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citation.

claim: Membrane tension and/or torsion is required to overcome the energy barrier to fission.
source: For instance, the super-constricted state of dynamin does not constrict the membrane sufficiently enough to reach the hemi-fission state (Sundborger et al., 2014) and membrane tension and/or torsion is required to overcome the energy barrier to fission (Bashkirov et al., 2008; Morlot et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: GTP hydrolysis induces constriction of the dynamin-amphiphysin helices as well as clustering.
source: In this study, we showed that GTP hydrolysis induces constriction of the dynamin-amphiphysin helices as well as clustering (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by HS-AFM data in Figure 3.

claim: Radial and longitudinal remodeling of the dynamin-amphiphysin helices may give local tension and/or torsion to the membrane tube at the edge of the clusters to drive membrane fission.
source: These radial and longitudinal remodeling of the dynamin-amphiphysin helices may give local tension and/or torsion to the membrane tube at the edge of the clusters to drive membrane fission.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for how clustering leads to fission.

claim: The dynamin-amphiphysin clusters may serve as a lipid diffusion barrier that causes friction leading to membrane scission.
source: Alternatively, the dynamin-amphiphysin clusters may serve as a lipid diffusion barrier that causes friction leading to membrane scission (Simunovic et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an alternative speculative mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Longitudinal rearrangement upon GTP hydrolysis similar to the cluster formation by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was observed in an EM study on the dynamics of dynamin with lipid nanotubes.
source: Longitudinal rearrangement upon GTP hydrolysis similar to the cluster formation by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was also observed in an EM study on the dynamics of dynamin with lipid nanotubes (Stowell et al., 1999) and more recently by HS-AFM analyses on dynamics of ΔPRD dynamin (Colom et al., 2017), suggesting that the longitudinal rearrangement is an intrinsic property of dynamin during membrane fission.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citation.

claim: Longitudinal rearrangement was observed by HS-AFM analyses on dynamics of ΔPRD dynamin.
source: Longitudinal rearrangement upon GTP hydrolysis similar to the cluster formation by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was also observed in an EM study on the dynamics of dynamin with lipid nanotubes (Stowell et al., 1999) and more recently by HS-AFM analyses on dynamics of ΔPRD dynamin (Colom et al., 2017), suggesting that the longitudinal rearrangement is an intrinsic property of dynamin during membrane fission.
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study supported by citation.

claim: The longitudinal rearrangement is an intrinsic property of dynamin during membrane fission.
source: Longitudinal rearrangement upon GTP hydrolysis similar to the cluster formation by the dynamin-amphiphysin complexes was also observed in an EM study on the dynamics of dynamin with lipid nanotubes (Stowell et al., 1999) and more recently by HS-AFM analyses on dynamics of ΔPRD dynamin (Colom et al., 2017), suggesting that the longitudinal rearrangement is an intrinsic property of dynamin during membrane fission.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar behavior in different studies.

claim: Amphiphysin enhances dynamin's GTPase activity in the presence of liposomes.
source: In our previous studies, we showed that amphiphysin enhances dynamin's GTPase activity in the presence of liposomes (Takei et al., 1999; Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the authors' prior work supported by citations.

claim: Tubular structures have long been known to be present in various synapses.
source: Tubular structures have long been known to be present in various synapses, and they are described as 'membrane tubules' (Heuser and Miledi, 1971), 'cisternae' (Heuser and Reese, 1973), 'synaptic tubules' (Samorajski et al., 1966) or 'anastomosing tubules' (Ekström von Lubitz, 1981).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: The tubules are enriched in endocytic proteins including dynamin, synaptojanin, amphiphysin, and endophilin.
source: The tubules are enriched in endocytic proteins including dynamin, synaptojanin, amphiphysin, and endophilin (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), and the presence of the tubules becomes more prominent when synapses are stimulated (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), or when membrane fission is blocked in dynamin 1 K.O. mice (Ferguson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: The presence of the tubules becomes more prominent when synapses are stimulated.
source: The tubules are enriched in endocytic proteins including dynamin, synaptojanin, amphiphysin, and endophilin (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), and the presence of the tubules becomes more prominent when synapses are stimulated (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), or when membrane fission is blocked in dynamin 1 K.O. mice (Ferguson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: The presence of the tubules becomes more prominent when membrane fission is blocked in dynamin 1 K.O. mice.
source: The tubules are enriched in endocytic proteins including dynamin, synaptojanin, amphiphysin, and endophilin (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), and the presence of the tubules becomes more prominent when synapses are stimulated (Fuchs et al., 2014; Takei et al., 1998), or when membrane fission is blocked in dynamin 1 K.O. mice (Ferguson et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citation.

claim: The tubular structures represent endocytic intermediate at which dynamin-amphiphysin-dependent synergic vesicle formation takes place in the synapse.
source: These findings strongly suggest that the tubular structures represent endocytic intermediate at which dynamin-amphiphysin-dependent synergic vesicle formation takes place in the synapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited observations about tubule composition and behavior.

claim: Other BAR domain proteins, endophilin and syndapin, are also implicated in synaptic vesicle recycling.
source: Besides amphiphysin, other BAR domain proteins, endophilin and syndapin, are also implicated in synaptic vesicle recycling (Dittman and Ryan, 2009; Koch et al., 2011; Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations.

claim: Endophilin potently inhibits the dynamin-mediated membrane fission by intercalating dynamin rungs and preventing their trans-interactions required for membrane fission.
source: Interestingly, recent study showed that endophilin potently inhibits the dynamin-mediated membrane fission by intercalating dynamin rungs and preventing their trans-interactions required for membrane fission (Hohendahl et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent study supported by citation.

claim: The dynamin-mediated membrane fission is inhibited when an excess of amphiphysin co-assembles with dynamin.
source: Although the dynamin-mediated membrane fission is also inhibited when an excess of amphiphysin co-assembles with dynamin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), it is rather stimulatory when the molar ratio of dynamin to amphiphsyin is around 1:1 (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and prior work.

claim: Dynamin-mediated membrane fission is stimulatory when the molar ratio of dynamin to amphiphysin is around 1:1.
source: Although the dynamin-mediated membrane fission is also inhibited when an excess of amphiphysin co-assembles with dynamin (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), it is rather stimulatory when the molar ratio of dynamin to amphiphsyin is around 1:1 (Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work supported by citation.
